newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ govt has no comment on latest Australian leak.
newsitem.headline: NZ govt has no comment on latest Australian leak.

text.p: New Zealand's top ministers, preparing to visit Australia at the weekend, declined to comment on Wednesday on a new leak of top secret documents from Canberra.
The latest report, the second leak within five days to show up apparent Australian concerns about New Zealand's external policies, slams Wellington's defence spending as "inadequate".
A spokesman for Prime Minister Jim Bolger's office declined to comment on the report and spokesmen for other ministries referred questions to Bolger's office.
Bolger, Treasurer Winston Peters and Finance Minister Bill Birch are all due to fly to Melbourne for scheduled bilateral meetings at various levels.

Peters, who also carries the title of Deputy Prime Minister, is the focus of both the defence document leaked on Wednesday and a detailed New Zealand section of a lengthy briefing paper on South Pacific economies and leaders revealed at the weekend.

Both documents -- marked 'AUSTEO', or Australian Eyes Only -- were prepared for Peters' counterpart Peter Costello ahead of a summit of economic ministers from the 16-member South Pacific Forum in Cairns earlier this month.
The latest 39-page report details a cabinet strategy of Australian ministers pressing the need for bigger military spending by their New Zealand counterparts at every opportunity.
It outlines concern at New Zealand's defence budget and Canberra's feeling that Australia carries an unfair share of the bilateral defence burden.
"Inadequate NZ defence funding might mean Australia was seen to be accepting a disproportionate share of the bilateral burden," the paper said.
The briefing goes on to say that even the latest draft of Wellington's upcoming defence review would see long-term defence stalled below 1990/91 levels.
Cabinet ministers have said a long-awaited Defence Assessment, initiated in 1996 and intended to outline future resources and funding, should be finished within weeks.
In parallel with this, the New Zealand Defence Force (NZDF) is working on a defence management plan to cut future costs.
Wellington has made clear its defence assessment will clarify whether or not it is going to take up an option to buy two more frigates from Australia which expires in November.
One of the first pair ordered was commissioned this week.
However, critics, including some ministers, have been saying for many months that the government ought to be looking at spending on much more than just more of the ANZAC-class ships.
The air force wants modern strike aircraft to replace its ageing Skyhawk fighters, as well as long-promised new Hercules transport planes, while the army wants new personnel carriers.
